The English still describes same-point vector addition and explicitly denies a particle path. The received parallelogram geometry remains semantically applicable; the new construction wording leaves geometric prerequisites unexplained.

independentPhysicsAssessment.assessment: Experimental origin and force evidence are retained without claiming one measurement establishes every property. Electrostatics is qualified by a chosen reference frame and a time-independent stationary source arrangement. The small, approximately stationary, nonperturbing probe and electric-force-only scope are retained. The text does not extend all electrostatic conclusions to changing fields.

For a fixed external field, electric force is signed probe charge times field vector. Reversing probe sign reverses force; division by that same nonzero signed charge leaves the field unchanged. The force excludes gravity. The definition and equations are correct, but the direction statement requires the zero-field qualification in EN67-R3 and reader scaffolding in EN67-R1.
independentPhysicsAssessment.arithmeticCheck: Read-only checks with a two-component nonzero field and opposite signed probes confirmed force reversal and unchanged force/charge quotient.

independentPhysicsAssessment.assessment: Finite-size neglect at the distances considered, homogeneous and isotropic properties, linear scaling, unchanged material state, ignored boundaries and local effects are explicitly present. The scalar epsilon formula is consistent with the intended ideal dielectric model, but 'material' and generic 'response' do not actually specify an insulating dielectric or explain its polarization. EN67-R2 requests that missing domain and physical meaning, not a formula change.

The source charge enters the magnitude through its absolute value. A positive q0 is chosen and repeated immediately before the preserved F/q0 magnitude formula. For that choice, absolute q0 equals q0 and cancels. The English explicitly requires the absolute probe charge when using a negative probe to calculate a magnitude. No erratum or unsigned-vector substitution is invented.
independentPhysicsAssessment.arithmeticCheck: Positive and negative source magnitudes agree; force magnitude divided by a negative signed probe gives the wrong sign, whereas dividing by its absolute value gives the field magnitude.

independentPhysicsAssessment.assessment: Force/charge has SI unit N/C. With epsilon0 as the dimensional vacuum constant and epsilon as relative permittivity, the SI expression has field dimensions; the CGSE expression belongs to a different electrostatic convention, not SI with a missing constant. The warning against mixing systems is correct. The text excludes the source's zero-distance point at the end. Identification and concrete explanation of the two epsilon symbols and the length/charge unit conventions remain missing in EN67-R2/R4.
independentPhysicsAssessment.arithmeticCheck: Doubling a nonzero distance gives one quarter of the magnitude; doubling the positive relative-permittivity factor halves it. These are arbitrary reviewer arithmetic checks, not new lesson data or calibration.

independentPhysicsAssessment.assessment: For a nonzero point source away from its position, outward positive-source and inward negative-source directions are correct. For a general field at a cancellation point, however, both field and electric force are zero and have no direction. The unconditional same/opposite-direction language in prose 9 does not state this exception.

The same probe and observation point are used, source positions and amounts are fixed, and the vacuum/linear electrostatic model is retained. Factoring the common signed probe charge from the force sum and dividing by the nonzero probe correctly gives the field vector sum. Opposing contributions cancel rather than requiring scalar magnitude addition. Source particles can still move and conductor charges redistribute; recalculation after source changes and exclusion of directly applying the rule to nonlinear media are explicit.
independentPhysicsAssessment.arithmeticCheck: Opposite two-component fields sum to zero, and the separately calculated signed forces equal the signed probe times their vector sum for either probe sign.

findings.evidence: The arrow/vector concept and signed charge are explained, but the first displayed equation introduces the letter F without an explicit force-vector key. No plain-language reading explains the equality sign, fraction bar or multiplication by juxtaposition; q>0 and q<0 are used without explaining greater-than/less-than zero. The source/test switch introduces q0 without explaining the lower zero as a label. Scalar E appears without an explicit no-arrow/magnitude key, and the factoring and division steps are only presented as equations.
findings.impact: A reader with no algebra cannot reliably connect the prose to the formula, distinguish a label from multiplication, decode the sign cases or understand why the common probe charge disappears. Preserved math tokens and correct expert algebra do not supply those prerequisites.
findings.requiredChange: Add short plain-English symbol keys and verbal readings at first use: F with its arrow names the electric-force vector; E with its arrow names field strength; a fraction bar means divide and an equality says both sides describe the same quantity; adjoining charge and field symbols mean multiplication. Explain greater/less than zero as positive/negative, that lower zero labels the probe rather than making its charge zero, and that E without an arrow is the nonnegative field size. Explain factoring as the same probe amount multiplying both contributions, and division as removing that common nonzero probe amount. Use a concrete verbal doubling or opposite-direction illustration rather than another unexplained equation.
findings.acceptance: A novice can read equations (8-11), (8-12), (8-13) and the superposition derivation aloud in ordinary words and distinguish source, probe, vector, magnitude and sign without consulting an earlier lesson.

findings.evidence: The formula is introduced for an ideal 'material, or medium' with homogeneous, isotropic and linear 'response'. Neither dielectric/insulating behavior nor the physical response being scaled is explained. 'The epsilon symbols denote the vacuum electric constant and the medium's relative permittivity' does not explicitly tell the reader which glyph is which, whether the relative factor has units, or how that factor changes the field.
findings.impact: The reader cannot know that this is the intended ideal insulating dielectric or vacuum model rather than an arbitrary material, including a conductor where source charges can rearrange. A generic response definition also leaves permittivity as a renamed technical term rather than a concrete physical idea.
findings.requiredChange: Explicitly identify the ideal insulating dielectric, or vacuum, and explain in simple words that charges bound inside the material shift slightly in response to a field rather than flowing freely as in a conductor. Keep all existing homogeneous/linear/isotropic, fixed-state, boundary and local-effect restrictions. Identify epsilon with the lower zero as the vacuum constant and plain epsilon as the unit-free relative factor; explain that vacuum has relative factor one and that, for the same fixed source and distance in this model, a larger relative factor reduces the field by that factor. Do not add a new numerical value for the vacuum constant.
findings.acceptance: The reader can identify the two epsilon symbols, explain the intended material model and state the qualitative effect of relative permittivity while retaining the exact source equations.

findings.evidence: The text states that E and F point in the same direction for a positive probe and opposite directions for a negative probe without restricting that statement to a nonzero field. Its later opposite-push example explicitly allows complete cancellation.
findings.impact: At a cancellation point, both field and electric force are zero and neither has a direction. The current unconditional wording gives an incorrect direction rule in a case this lesson itself permits.
findings.requiredChange: Qualify the direction comparison as applying when the field is nonzero, and say in ordinary words that complete cancellation gives zero field and zero electric force, with no direction arrow to assign.
findings.acceptance: The sign rule remains correct for a nonzero field, and the reader does not assign a direction to a zero resultant. No displayed math token needs changing.

findings.evidence: 'A newton measures force and a coulomb measures charge' names the quantities but does not concretely read 'per coulomb' as force for one unit of probe charge. The point-charge formula does not state the SI length unit for r. CGSE is only named; the explanation says its units/constants differ without identifying the older centimetre-gram-second electrostatic convention or explaining why the smaller-looking formula cannot accept SI numbers.
findings.impact: A novice cannot select consistent length and charge units, or tell whether (8-14) is an alternative SI shortcut. 'Do not mix' is a correct warning but not enough to understand or obey it without unit-system prerequisites.
findings.requiredChange: Explain per coulomb as electric force for one coulomb of positive probe charge and relate a doubled probe amount to a doubled force without changing the field. State that the SI point-charge expression uses charge in coulombs, distance in metres and the matching vacuum constant. Briefly identify CGSE as the older centimetre-gram-second electrostatic convention with its own charge and field units and constants; explain that the same physical quantity has a different numerical expression when the measuring unit changes. A full conversion table or extra exercises are not required.
findings.acceptance: The reader understands what the field unit means and why the two preserved equations must not be evaluated with a mixture of SI and CGSE numbers.

findings.evidence: The text defines a parallelogram and says to 'copy each along the opposite side', then selects 'the diagonal from their shared starting point'. It does not define a diagonal or identify the far opposite corner, and the copying instruction relies on knowing how the opposite sides are located. The learner is explicitly assumed to have no geometry prerequisites.
findings.impact: The reader may understand that arrows combine yet still be unable to reconstruct which line is the resultant in Figure 114. This is a text-context instructional gap, not evidence of a failed figure pixel or geometry gate.
findings.requiredChange: Describe the construction concretely: keep the two arrows' tails at the observation point; from each arrow tip draw a copy of the other arrow, preserving its length and direction; the copies meet at the far corner. Define a diagonal as a line joining opposite corners and identify the resultant as the arrow from the original shared tail to that far corner. Retain the explicit warning that this is not a particle path.
findings.acceptance: A child unfamiliar with parallelograms or diagonals can identify the component arrows, shared origin, copied sides and resultant from the words and the unchanged figure, without newly asserting calibrated lengths or angles.
